extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, inventors, and legal practitioners advising on patent rights, infringement, and remedies
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules for establishing, defending, and obtaining remedies for patent infringement (what constitutes infringement, evidence and pleading requirements, and equitable vs legal remedies). Aimed at practitioners handling patent suits and injunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignability and bequest of patent-right
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee may bequeath the patent in any manner he pleases; if he makes no will, it is assets in the hands of his administrator. Patents can be assigned in trust and, by act of parliament, made assignable to more than five persons or divisible into many shares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: trusts declared in Cartwright's patent; Koops's patent interest was divided into sixty shares by act of parliament. Where Parliament intervenes to enlarge assignability, a proviso often preserves every legal objection to the patent as against the act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licences and licencees' rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee may grant licences to persons to use the invention; in the event of infringement of the patent-right, all who have licences may maintain actions for damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licencees generally have standing to sue for infringement. The patentee need not part wholly with his patent to permit use by others via licences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for parliamentary extension or enlargement
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament may extend a patent's term or increase the number of persons that may be interested when the patentee's application, labour, and expense have been so great that he has not received adequate reward; or when expensive improvements, family incapacity, or undertaking magnitude justify relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative relief has been granted for various causes (e.g., expensive improvements, inventor's death leaving family unable to proceed, undertakings too large for five persons). When such Acts are passed, they commonly include clauses preserving existing legal objections to the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: No exclusive property in secret discoveries absent special protection
rubrics_metrics.description: A person keeping a discovery secret and using or vending the manufacture without a patent cannot claim an exclusive legal property in that subject; courts will not generally prevent others from making use of such manufactures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: (1) If fraud is practised in getting at the secret or one represents his article to be the same as the secret article (misrepresentation), the secret-holder may obtain damages or an injunction; (2) contractual undertakings (see separate criterion) can protect secrets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual protection of disclosed secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: If a man agrees to inform another of a secret invention, and the other binds himself by a penalty not to avail himself or take undue advantage of the communication, the informer may maintain an action for breach of that contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is distinct from patent law — it enforces contractual obligations to keep and not exploit trade secrets disclosed under agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: What amounts to an infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the defendant's act is an infringement is a question for the jury. The making or using of any the least part of the manufacture is an infringement; if the defendant's article is of different form or made with slight and immaterial additions or substitutions, yet the manufactures are really and substantially the same, the patentee is entitled to a remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: slight departures made solely to evade the patent are frauds upon the patent. If the defendant has not worked according to the specification, that is open to proof. The inquiry is whether the defendants' mode of working has been essentially or substantially different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection limited to well-specified parts vs speculative matter
rubrics_metrics.description: If certain articles are well specified and others are only mentioned in the specification as speculative matter (not intended as perfect instruments), the speculative parts cannot be protected and may be infringed with impunity; but infringement of the well-specified parts cannot be excused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mr. Watt inserted imperfect articles as speculative; those cannot be monopolised. Inventors must be careful to identify what parts they actually claim as perfected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of combination patents and partial use
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent is for combinations and proportions producing a new effect, the use of any of the ingredients singly, or in partial combination omitting some, may not be covered as such; yet if a partial combination or differently proportioned composition produces substantially the same result, it may constitute an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination depends on the nature of the claim: patents for a new combination are distinct from patents on individual ingredients or processes; slight departures that nevertheless reproduce the claimed effect can be infringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available remedies for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies include an action at common law for damages (action on the case) and proceedings in equity for an injunction and an account of profits. The Court of Chancery can restrain further use and order an account; common law provides damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of forum: equity is often preferred for immediate restraint and accounting; law actions may be pursued concurrently or subsequently. Even a patent that is void in itself may give rise to actions on the case until it is cancelled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee and joinder in suits
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent has been assigned, the assignee may sue alone, or the assignee and the patentee may join in the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignment does not prevent the original patentee from joining; standing to sue vests in assignee as legal owner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleadings and procedural formalities in infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a grant by letters patent is pleaded it ought to be shown under what seal it is made; the declaration must state the patent to be under the great seal. A profert is made and recited, but oyer of the patent is not allowed (they are matters of record). Venue for such actions must be laid in the county of Middlesex. The usual plea is 'not guilty', which puts the declaration in issue; a defendant may demur if the patent is void on the face of the declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful drafting of declarations is required; precedents exist (e.g., King v. Arkwright). Demurrer or plea strategy depends on whether patent appears void on its face.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and required evidence by the patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff must be prepared to prove material allegations: that the invention in all parts to which the patent applies is new and useful, that he is the inventor, and that the specification is sufficient in law. A plaintiff must give some evidence to show what his invention was (slight evidence is sufficient to make a prima facie case), after which the defendant must falsify the specification or the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sufficiency: experienced and intelligent men versed in the art who have never heard of the invention is good prima facie evidence of novelty; but if one witness states prior use the novelty is destroyed. Slight evidence of operation in the manner specified may suffice to shift burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of infringement by inspection and comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspection and comparison of manufactures may provide evidence of infringement. If defendant refuses inspection and the defendant's product agrees in all qualities with a product made by the plaintiff's method, that is prima facie evidence it was made by that method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may order inspection of manufactories (especially where infringement is secret). It is prudent to seek equitable inspection orders to avoid difficulties proving infringement by comparison alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity practice for injunctions and accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court of Chancery will, in aid of the common law, grant injunctions and order accounts where the patent-owner has exclusive possession; it may grant an ex parte injunction on filing the bill and affidavits, commanding the defendant to refrain from use or to keep an account until validity and infringement are determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions: where the patent is very recent or validity is seriously disputed the court will generally require the patentee to establish validity at law before acting on its own notion; affidavits for ex parte injunctions should state particulars of the alleged infringement and the applicant's belief that he is the original inventor. Separate bills are required for each distinct invasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant's equity-side rights and answers
rubrics_metrics.description: On receiving a bill, the defendant must bring in an answer (usually verified by affidavit) stating facts showing either that the patent is not a good one, or that he has not infringed it. The defendant may plead matters in equity or demur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If affidavits are very contradictory, the court may dismiss the suit; otherwise it may continue the injunction and direct an issue at law to try validity, or order accounts to be kept pending litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of judgments and continuing suits until cancellation
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a patentee is defeated in one action, he may maintain fresh suits against other infringers; conversely, even if a defendant succeeds, the patentee may still proceed in fresh suits until the letters patent are actually cancelled by scire facias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a grant is protected until cancelled (for the honour of the grantor, the King), public means (scire facias) exist to destroy a bad patent. Parties may also seek costs against those who alleged a right which could not be supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for granting or dissolving injunctions (equity discretion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lord Chancellor (or equity court) will use discretion: where possession and validity appear established, the court may grant or revive injunctions and order accounts; but if there is strong doubt as to validity the court may refuse to revive an injunction and instead direct accounts to be kept until the legal questions are tried.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity balances the urgency of preventing further infringement against the risk of enforcing an invalid patent; historical practice required particularity in affidavits (what alleged infringement consisted of and that it worked according to specification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate bills required for separate invasions
rubrics_metrics.description: For each distinct invasion of the patent there must be separate bills filed in equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should file separate suits for distinct acts of infringement rather than lumping multiple invasions into a single bill.

rubrics_metrics.name: When specification defects or concealment affect litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is alleged that the patentee intended to conceal the invention or made an obscure specification (e.g., to prevent foreigners using it), that fact is admissible and may undermine the patentee's claim; the patentee admitted an obscure specification to avoid disclosure may be disadvantaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will examine the specification by reading it in for validity; palpable variance between specification and title may be fatal on the face of the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical procedural rules (venue, evidence, demurrer, profert)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural rules include: venue must be Middlesex (patent tested at Westminster); profert of letters patent is made and recited but oyer is not allowed; by statute exemplifications of letters patent may be used in pleading and evidence; defendant may demur where the declaration shows the patent is void on its face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory changes permit exemplifications to be shewn forth instead of originals; practitioners must follow local procedural formalities in drafting and proof.
